established_findings.statement: LLMs can be used to translate high-level operator intent into network configuration artifacts in controlled/experimental settings using fine-tuning and in‑context learning.
limitations: Evaluations reported are in controlled settings; vendor/CLI and protocol coverage is limited.
Performance depends on fine-tuning / in-context examples and may not generalize to unseen production topologies.

established_findings.statement: LLMs can serve as configuration validators / misconfiguration detectors with non-trivial effectiveness, when combined with prompt engineering and example data.
limitations: Detection efficacy varies by model and configuration domain; authors report blind spots (e.g., some misconfiguration classes are detected poorly).
LLM nondeterminism and hallucination risk require output checks.

established_findings.statement: LLMs can propose repairs for infrastructure-as-code and configuration files, often reducing automated scanner alarms, but a notable fraction of suggested fixes are incorrect or hallucinated.
limitations: Reported metrics show high reduction in alarm counts but manual verification finds a non-negligible false-fix (hallucination) rate.
Human-in-the-loop validation was required/used in evaluated pipelines.

established_findings.statement: Benchmarking frameworks for LLMs on network-configuration tasks have been proposed (e.g., NetLLMBench) to integrate prompt engineering with emulation and closed-loop validation.
limitations: Existing benchmark frameworks are early-stage and do not yet establish community-wide standardized suites or broad ecological validity.

established_findings.statement: Retrieval-augmentation, external tool/middleware use, and validator-assisted generate–validate–repair architectures are proposed and empirically used to reduce hallucinations and improve factual/structural grounding of LLM outputs.
limitations: Proposed mitigations vary in evaluation depth; their effectiveness in realistic, multi-vendor NetOps pipelines is not yet fully characterized.

established_findings.statement: Surveys and empirical studies consistently identify major failure modes for LLMs relevant to NetOps: hallucinations, non-determinism, prompt sensitivity, and concerns about evaluation validity.
limitations: The cited analyses cover broad LLM applications (code, V&V, evaluation methodology); direct quantitative NetOps-specific failure-rate generalization requires domain-specific studies.

unresolved_questions.statement: To what extent do LLM-based NetOps systems generalize across vendor CLIs, routing/switching protocols, and large/heterogeneous production topologies?
unresolved_questions.evidence_type: survey / V&V review highlighting external validity gaps
limitations: Surveys note external validity concerns but do not provide definitive cross-vendor empirical estimates.
Requires systematic multi-vendor, large-topology experiments not present in supplied records.

unresolved_questions.statement: What are the best-practice integration patterns and empirical effectiveness when combining LLM generation with formal network verification tools (e.g., closed-loop use of verifiers) in NetOps pipelines?
limitations: Existing work calls for such integration but empirical studies demonstrating robust combos at scale are not present among the supplied records.

unresolved_questions.statement: What operational safety and human-in-the-loop governance policies are necessary to make agentic LLM NetOps acceptable in production (metrics, latency, approval workflows, liability)?
limitations: The records diagnose governance and oversight challenges but stop short of validated operational prescriptions for NetOps.

candidate_gaps.statement: There is a need for standardized, reproducible, community-accepted NetOps LLM benchmarks that cover multi-vendor CLIs, realistic topologies, and safety-relevant failure modes; existing proposals are nascent.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: benchmark proposal + surveys calling out evaluation gaps
limitations: NetLLMBench exists as an initial framework, but community adoption and coverage breadth remain limited per surveys.

candidate_gaps.statement: Empirical quantification of hallucination-induced operational risk in NetOps (e.g., misconfiguration causing outages or security exposures) is underexplored in the supplied literature.
candidate_gaps.evidence_type: empirical repair paper + hallucination analyses + V&V survey
limitations: Some papers measure repair/hallucination rates for IaC and code, but explicit linkage from LLM hallucinations to quantified NetOps operational risk in production scenarios is missing.

candidate_gaps.statement: Comparative evaluations of mitigation strategies (RAG, tool calling, formal verification, multi-agent SOP constraints) specifically for NetOps workflows are limited.
limitations: Mitigation techniques are proposed and demonstrated in adjacent domains; head-to-head NetOps-specific comparisons are not present among the supplied records.

excluded_claims: LLMs are proven production-ready to autonomously manage enterprise networks without human oversight (unsupported: supplied records show controlled experiments, partial fixes, and notable hallucination/validation gaps).
Retrieval-augmentation (RAG) or tool-calling fully eliminates hallucinations in NetOps settings (unsupported: surveys and empirical studies show mitigation benefits but not complete elimination).
LLMs achieve near-perfect automatic repair of network configurations with zero incorrect/hallucinated fixes (unsupported: IaC repair and SecConfig papers report non-negligible incorrect-fix rates).

There is conclusive evidence in the supplied records that integration of LLMs with formal network verifiers (e.g., Batfish/NetPlumber) has been empirically validated at production scale (unsupported by supplied records).
